props.title: The Freshman
props.initialSlug: A mob deal gone hilariously wrong.

sections.content: The Freshman brilliantly pairs Matthew Broderick with Marlon Brando in a clever satire of The Godfather (1972). Brando essentially parodies his iconic Don Corleone role as Carmine Sabatini, a mobster running an exotic food smuggling operation. The film's genius lies in how it balances comedy with genuine tension, while commenting on both film history and 1990s materialism. Director Andrew Bergman, who wrote Blazing Saddles (1974), brings his sharp satirical eye to organized crime tropes.

sections.content: The film fits perfectly into the wave of mob comedy crossovers that emerged in the late 1980s and early 1990s. While Goodfellas (1990) was taking a gritty, realistic approach to the genre, films like Oscar (1991) and Analyze This (1999) found humor in gangster conventions. The Freshman stands out by directly incorporating film history through Brando's meta-performance.

What makes The Freshman particularly special is its commentary on privileged youth encountering the criminal underworld. Like Risky Business (1983) before it, the film explores how an innocent student gets seduced by easy money. Broderick's Clark Kellogg serves as our stand-in, moving from wide-eyed film student to reluctant criminal apprentice, echoing his role in Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986). SUBHEAD: The Brando Factor

sections.content: Marlon Brando's performance deserves special attention. After largely withdrawing from major roles following Apocalypse Now (1979), his turn in The Freshman showed he could still command the screen while poking fun at his legendary status. The film works as both homage to and satire of The Godfather, with Brando gleefully sending up his most famous role.
